title: Simulating Majorana fermions in black hole with Ising Models
authors: John Vienn A. Estremadura, Kristian Hauser A. Villegas
abstract: Quantum field theory (QFT) in curved spacetime has led to profound predictions, including the Unruh effect and Hawking radiation, yet their direct observation remains extraordinarily challenging because of their extremely weak signatures. Here, we show that the transverse-field Ising model provides a quantum simulator for Majorana fermions in a Schwarzschild black hole background. Remarkably, different coordinate representations of the same spacetime-Schwarzschild, tortoise, Kruskal, and conformally flat-map onto distinct microscopic Ising spin models. Despite their microscopic differences, these models converge in the continuum limit to the same Majorana field theory, exhibiting an emergent form of general covariance. This provides a rare example of a fundamental symmetry of general relativity arising as an emergent property of a condensed matter system. We further demonstrate how black hole particle production can be simulated and detected through spin correlation measurements, and discuss experimental platforms capable of realizing these models. Our work establishes a practical route for investigating fermionic QFT in curved spacetime using controllable quantum many-body systems and tabletop experiments.
summary: The paper demonstrates that Majorana fermions in curved spacetime can be simulated using the transverse-field Ising model. By showing that different coordinate choices lead to distinct but equivalent spin Hamiltonians, the authors establish a practical route to study black hole physics on tabletop quantum simulators. This work highlights how fundamental symmetries of gravity can emerge from condensed matter systems.
main_problem: Investigating Quantum Field Theory (QFT) phenomena, such as Hawking radiation, in curved spacetime backgrounds.
main_result: The authors show that different coordinate representations of the same black hole spacetime map onto distinct but equivalent microscopic Ising spin models, demonstrating emergent general covariance.
method: Analog simulation by mapping QFT on curved spacetime to controllable quantum many-body systems (spin chains).
model_or_system: The system uses the transverse-field Ising model applied to Majorana fermions in a Schwarzschild black hole background. The Hamiltonian is derived from the continuum limit of lattice spin models.
key_observables: Spin correlation measurements used to simulate and detect black hole particle production, which are compared against Fermi-Dirac distributions.
important_parameters: The Hawking temperature ($k_B T/J$) and the Majorana mass ($m$), which governs the particle number expectation value.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on taking the continuum limit approximation when mapping lattice models to field theory, and using $\zeta(t, x) = 0$ for simplification in some derivations.
figures_summary: Figure 2(b) shows that the simulated particle number follows a Fermi-Dirac distribution whose temperature scales with the Schwarzschild radius; Figure 2(a) discusses oscillations related to finite Kruskal time or discretization effects.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the mapping from QFT in curved spacetime to spin models, then analyzes how different coordinate systems (Schwarzschild vs. conformally flat) yield distinct but equivalent microscopic Hamiltonians, and finally applies this framework to calculate particle production via correlation measurements.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete realization where fundamental symmetries of General Relativity emerge from the dynamics of controllable quantum many-body systems like trapped ions or Rydberg arrays, making it highly relevant for AMO physicists studying emergent physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Transverse magnetic field as a function of position for spin systems generated using (a) Schwarzschild, (b) tortoise, and (c) Kruskal coordinates, plotted for various values of the parameter mϵ. The black hole horizon is set at rs = 1.

FIG. 2. Numerical simulation of the fermion number of the Kruskal vacuum using the Ising model, as measured by an observer in tortoise coordinates. Panels (a) and (b) show the fermion number for varying Schwarzschild radius rs as a function of the mode number and the energy eigenvalue, respectively. The inset in (b) shows the energy eigenvalues as a function of the mode number. Panel (c) shows the fermion number as a function of the mode number for varying Majorana mass m.
